title: The Brass Vessel
subtitle: A king, a ring, and seventy-two things that would not kneel
blurb: Where the story starts: Solomon seals seventy-two spirits in a jar of brass, and somebody breaks it open.

segments.t: Somewhere under Babylon there is a lake. Nobody has found it. That has never stopped anyone from telling you exactly what is at the bottom.

At the bottom, the story goes, there was a jar. A vessel of brass, about as tall as a child, sealed at the neck with a lid of lead, and stamped with a seal that nothing inside could bear to look at. And inside it, folded up like smoke, were seventy-two spirits and every soldier who served them.
These be the seventy-two mighty Kings and Princes which King Solomon commanded into a Vessel of Brass, together with their Legions.

That voice is the book. You will hear it again. Whenever it speaks, those are the real words, copied by hand in the sixteen hundreds, printed in nineteen oh four. I will never put words in its mouth. I am the other voice. Call me the Keeper. I hold the lamp, and I tell you where the stairs are.

Good evening. This is The Brass Vessel. Twelve nights with one of the strangest books ever written in English. It has many names. The Lemegeton. The Clavicula Salomonis Regis. Most people call it the Lesser Key of Solomon. It is a catalogue of demons. Their names, their ranks, their faces, and what each one is good for.

Before we go down, three honest things. One. I am not going to teach you to summon anything, and I am not going to tell you this is real. Two. I am not going to tell you it is nonsense, either, because for four hundred years serious, frightened, clever people did not think so, and their fear is a kind of evidence about them. Three. You do not need to know anything. Not Latin, not scripture, not what a grimoire is. A grimoire is a book of magic. There. You are caught up.

threshold.q: So tell me, before I open the cover. Why did you come down here tonight?

opts.label: I want the history
opts.reply: Good. Then you will like the manuscripts, the forgeries, and the doctor who published a list of demons to prove that witches were innocent. History is the best part. History is where the bodies are. Keep your pencil sharp.

opts.label: I want to feel something
opts.reply: Honest. Most people say history and mean this. Then listen with the lights low. The book was built to be felt. Every name in it was written to be spoken aloud, in the dark, by someone whose hands were shaking. We will go slowly.

opts.label: I think it's nonsense
opts.reply: Excellent. Stay that way. The first great printer of this list was a sceptic, and he printed it anyway, because he could not look away. Doubt is not a wall against this book. Doubt is how most people get in.

segments.t: Then we begin where the book begins. With a king.

Solomon. Son of David, king in Jerusalem, some three thousand years ago. In scripture he is the wise one. He asks for wisdom instead of riches and receives both. He builds the Temple. That is the Solomon of Sunday school. But there is a second Solomon, who lives in the margins. And the second Solomon is a magician.

The idea is old. By the first century, a historian named Josephus is already writing that God taught Solomon the art of casting out demons, and that he left behind incantations that still worked. A few centuries later, someone writes a wild little book called the Testament of Solomon. In it, a demon is stealing the wages and the life of a boy who works on the Temple. Solomon prays. And an angel hands him a ring.

Take, O Solomon, king, son of David, the gift which the Lord God has sent thee. With it thou shalt lock up all the demons of the earth, male and female; and with their help thou shalt build up Jerusalem.

Read that last line again in your head. With their help. Solomon does not destroy the demons. He hires them. He stamps each one with the ring, asks its name, asks what it does, asks which angel it fears, and then he puts it to work cutting stone. The Temple of God, in this story, is built by a chain gang of devils. And notice the method. Name. Office. Weakness. That is an interview. That is a filing system. Remember it. The whole Lesser Key is that interview, written down seventy-two times.

So where does the brass vessel come in? Here is how the Lesser Key tells it, in a few plain lines near the end of its first book. Solomon gathers the seventy-two greatest spirits. Kings, dukes, princes. And he shuts them in the jar. And the book is careful to tell you why.
And it is to be noted that Solomon did this because of their pride, for he never declared other reason why he thus bound them.

Because of their pride. Not murder. Not plague. Pride. I have always found that a little thrilling. Seventy-two beings who were asked to bow, and would not. Then the king seals the jar, and by divine power drives it down into a deep lake, or a hole, in Babylon. And that should be the end.

It is not the end, because of treasure hunters. The people of Babylon see a king go to enormous trouble to sink a sealed brass jar, and they reach the only sensible conclusion. Gold. So they wade into the lake, and they haul it up, and they break the seal.
But when they had broken it open, out flew the Chief Spirits immediately, with their Legions following them; and they were all restored to their former places.

All of them, home again. All except one, called Belial, who climbed into a statue and began answering prayers, which is its own kind of joke. We will meet him on the fifth night. But understand what that ending does. It turns a myth into a manual. If the seventy-two are loose, then they are out there now. And if Solomon wrote down their names and their seals, then anyone holding the book is holding the lid of the jar.

threshold.q: Put yourself on that shore. The jar is in front of you, green with age, and something inside is very quiet. What do you do?

opts.label: Break the seal
opts.reply: Of course you do. So did they. Every person who has ever opened this book has broken that seal, a little. I only ask that you notice the moment. That small cold drop in the stomach. That is the oldest feeling this book sells.

opts.label: Read the seal first
opts.reply: Careful. I like that. That is the magician's answer, as it happens. The whole art, as the book describes it, is reading before touching. Names first. Circles first. The ones who rushed are not the ones who wrote the manuscripts.

opts.label: Walk away
opts.reply: Wise. And yet here you are, still listening. Walking away from the jar and walking away from the story about the jar are different skills. Very few people have the second one. I certainly do not.

segments.t: So let us do the thing properly, and read one name. The first. The book opens its list without any ceremony at all. No warning, no preface. Just this.

The First Principal Spirit is a King ruling in the East, called Bael. He maketh thee to go Invisible. He ruleth over sixty-six Legions of Infernal Spirits. He appeareth in divers shapes, sometimes like a Cat, sometimes like a Toad, and sometimes like a Man, and sometimes all these forms at once. He speaketh hoarsely.

Bael. A king in the east, with sixty-six legions. He comes as a cat, or a toad, or a man, or all three at once, and he speaks hoarsely. I love that the book bothers to tell you about his voice. And his gift is invisibility. Look at your grimoire now. His seal has just appeared in it. Every spirit I introduce will be kept there, so you can go back and look them in the eye.

And notice the shape of that entry, because you are going to hear it seventy-one more times. A number. A rank. A name. A shape. A gift. A count of soldiers. It reads like a personnel file. That is the secret charm of the Lesser Key. It is not a scream. It is paperwork. Somebody sat down and made Hell into an office directory, and it is so calm about it that you start to believe the building exists.

One more thing about Bael, and then I will let you go. His name is older than this book. Much older. Thousands of years before anyone drew his seal, there was a storm god on the coast of Canaan, a rider of clouds, and his title was Baal. Lord. How a god of rain ends up as a hoarse king with a toad's head is one of the best stories we have, and I am saving it for the ninth night.

Tomorrow, the book itself. Because the Lesser Key is not one book. It is five, stitched together, and only the first is about demons. We will open the oldest copies, the ones in the British Library with the cramped brown ink, and ask the awkward question. Who actually wrote this?
Until then. The jar is open. The first name has been said. Seventy-one to go. Mind the stairs on your way up. And if you hear something hoarse behind you, do not worry. He is only being polite.

glossary.def: The traditional name for the Lesser Key of Solomon, a seventeenth-century English collection of five books of ritual magic. Nobody is sure what the word means.
A handbook of magic. The word is related to grammar: to people who could not read, any book of rules looked like sorcery.
A Greek text from the first centuries of the common era in which Solomon uses a magic ring to interrogate demons and force them to build the Temple. An ancestor of the Lesser Key.
In legend, a signet ring given to Solomon by an angel, engraved with a seal that compels spirits to obey. Later imagined as a pentagram or hexagram.
The sealed jar in which Solomon is said to have imprisoned the seventy-two spirits before sinking it in a lake in Babylon.
